title: Same Average, Different Spread
objective: After this level you can explain why two sets with the same average can be very different, and measure the gap with the range.
summary: Two sets can share an average yet differ in spread. The range, largest minus smallest, measures it quickly, but it uses only two values.

cards.headline: Two classes both average 70 on a test. Are they the same?
cards.body: In one, the scores were 40, 70 and 100. In the other, 69, 70 and 71. Same mean, very different rooms.

cards.headline: The average isn't the whole story
cards.body: In the first class, one student scored 30 below the mean and another 30 above it. In the second, everyone sat within a point of 70. The mean cannot tell those rooms apart. That is why a good summary also reports how spread out the values are: two sets can share a mean and still look nothing alike.

cards.headline: The range: biggest minus smallest
cards.body: The simplest measure of spread is the range: subtract the smallest value from the largest. First class: 100 − 40 = 60 points. Second class: 71 − 69 = 2 points. One more number, and suddenly the two rooms look as different as they really are.

cards.fact: The range looks at only two values.
cards.context: It uses just the largest and the smallest and ignores everything in between. So a single outlier at either end can stretch it, even if every other value sits tight. Handy for a quick look; for a fuller picture you need a measure that listens to every value. That is next level.

cards.headline: Spread: the range
learned: Same mean can hide different spread
The range uses only two values

questions.prompt: How do you find the range of a set of values?

options.label: Add them up and divide by how many
Find the value in the middle of the list
Subtract the smallest value from the largest
Count how often the top value appears
options.rationale: Counting how often gives the mode idea, not the range.

questions.explanation: The range is the largest value minus the smallest: 100 − 40 = 60 for the first class.

questions.prompt: Class A scored 40, 70 and 100; Class B scored 69, 70 and 71. What is the difference?

options.label: Class A has the higher mean
Class B has the bigger range
Same mean, but Class A is far more spread out
There is no difference, since the means match

questions.explanation: Both means are 70, but A's range is 60 points and B's is 2: same center, very different spread.

questions.prompt: Why can one outlier, like those in Level 15, distort the range so easily?

options.label: The range is a kind of median
options.rationale: The range is a spread, not a middle value.

options.label: The range uses only the largest and smallest values
The range counts the most common value
Outliers are always removed before the range is found
options.rationale: Not always; that is why they can distort it.

questions.explanation: An outlier is by nature the largest or smallest value, and those are the only two the range uses.
